title: Decision, Decision!
passageHtml:
READING PASSAGE 2

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 15–28, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

Decision, Decision!

Research explores when we can make a vital decision quickly and when we need to proceed more deliberately.

A A In about 400 BC, a complex knot was used to secure an oxcart to a pole in Gordium, a place in the country we now call Turkey, according to a common folk tale. The knot was so complex that anyone who could undo it would be crowned the Asian king. The knot would never come undone, however, despite all best efforts. Alexander the Great, the renowned ancient Greek leader, cut the knot with his sword instead of wasting time trying to figure out how to untie it, and then consequently conquered Asia, according to the legend. Solving difficult problems with delightfully simple actions has since been known as a ‘Gordian solution.’

B B These simple solutions have often lacked appeal to psychological researchers who study how we make decisions. More complex decisionmaking processes are important when shielding people from the risk of ‘groupthinking’, according to Decision Making, a book from 1977 by the ‘conflict model’ psychologists Leon Mann and Irving Janis. Suboptimal or even disastrous decisions would be made without investigating, reinvestigating, considering, reconsidering, or judging many possibilities and relevant details. A famous American politician made a particular decision about foreign relations in the 60s that has frequently been cited as an example of the dangers of failing to fully consider all available possibilities, even if the opposite is true of a later decision that the same leader made which showed evidence of the benefit of thoughtful deliberation. Both problems demanded attention and were granted thorough contemplation by the politicians involved, according to University of British Columbia psychologist Peter Suedfield and Stanford Graduate School of Business psychologist Roderick Kramer, who discovered that the process of deliberation was nearly identical in each case, despite the historical view that the second decision was the correct one.

C C Simple decisions are just as effective as more complex ones, generally speaking, if we judge by the evidence offered by political and organisational science. The notion that simple or quick decisions are more frequently correct than careful deliberation, popularized by Blink, a 2005 bestselling book by Malcolm Gladwell, has been backed by a growing collection of research studies.

D D Gladwell's influential book is echoed by University of Amsterdam researcher Ap Dijksterhuis, who, along with his colleagues, has published an article called Making the Right Choice: the Deliberationwithoutattention Effect. The authors suggest that cognitive resources are necessary for the most effective acts of conscious deliberation. Decisionmaking quality decreases as the complexity of the decision increases, since the addition of complexity demands greater and greater cognitive resources. Our cognitive capabilities are tested by more complex decisions. No cognitive resources, however, are required for unconscious decisions (‘deliberation without attention’ in the terminology of the researchers), and therefore effectiveness is not enhanced by added complexity. Conscious deliberation increases our power to make simple decisions, but this is not the case for decisions of greater complexity, even if this conclusion might seem to be counterintuitive to some.

E E Dijksterhuis reports four simple but elegant studies supporting this argument. In one, participants assessed the quality of four hypothetical cars by considering either four attributes (a simple task) or 12 attributes (a complex task). Among participants who considered four attributes, those who were allowed to engage in undistracted deliberative thought did better at discriminating between the best and worst cars. Those who were distracted and thus unable to deliberate had to rely on their unconscious thinking and did less well. The opposite pattern emerged when people considered 12 criteria. In this case, conscious deliberation led to inferior discrimination and poor decisions.

F F In another study, Dijksterhuis surveyed people shopping for clothes (‘simple’ products) and furniture (‘complex’ products). Compared with those who said they had deliberated long and hard, shoppers who bought with little conscious deliberation felt less happy with their simple clothing purchases but happier with the complex furniture purchases. Deliberation without attention actually produced better results as the decisions became more complex.

G G From there, however, the researchers take a big leap. They write: There is no reason to assume that the deliberationwithoutattention effect does not generalize to other types of choices—political, managerial or otherwise. In such cases, it should benefit the individual to think consciously about simple matters and to delegate thinking about more complicated matters to the unconscious.

H H This radical inference contradicts standard political and managerial theory but doubtlessly comforts those in politics and management who always find the simple solution to the complex problem an attractive proposition. Indeed, one believes that many of our political leaders already embrace this wisdom.

I I As social psychologist Kurt Lewin (18901947) noted, a ‘good’ decision that nobody respects is actually bad. His classic studies of decision making showed that participating in deliberative processes makes people more likely to abide by the results. The issue here is that when we believe political decision makers made mistakes, it is the relation between their political beliefs and our own, rather than psychology which is at fault.
